newsitem.title: USA: Russian banker expects Minfin bond defreeze soon.
newsitem.headline: Russian banker expects Minfin bond defreeze soon.

text.p: Some tranches of Russian Minfin bonds, currently frozen pending investigation of theft charges, should be unfrozen before the end of the year, said Dmitri Mozgin, senior general manager of Vneshtorgbank.
"We expect quick defreezing of Minfin bonds, because the prime minister has issued instructions to settle the matter immediately," he told the "Investing in Russia" seminar.
"By the end of the year they will be released," he predicted.
Vneshtorgbank is a major depository of Minfin bonds. About $74 million of MinFin bonds are known to be frozen -- some of which had been stolen in the breakaway republic of Chechnya.
The probe of the missing Minfin bonds apparenly rose from "misunderstanding" between different law enforcement authorities, Mozgin said.
Unlike missing Minfin bonds during the war in Chechnya, the bonds under the latest investigation are safe in the vaults of depository banks, he said. "They are not stolen."

On November 5, the Russian government called on judicial authorities to review recent freezes of MinFin bonds. First Deputy Prime Minister Vladimir Potanin's office said the Interior Ministry and Prosecutor-General's office were urged to refrain from any actions which could damage bondholders' rights.
The "scandal" apparently rose from overlapping jurisdictions of civil and criminal codes, he said, adding that the civil code which guarantees investors' rights should prevail.
Mozgin explained that the bonds came under criminal investigation because the serial numbers of some Minfin bonds were allegedly used for nubulous transactions.

Under criminal law police may freeze bonds which are said to be stolen, but under civil law bonds may not be seized from owners who acquired them in good faith. Judicial authorities have been asked to draw up proposals to reconcile the differences in civil and criminal laws. The proposals would then be submitted to parliament as an amendment to existing legislation.

Also speaking at the seminar, Alexander Kolesknikov, deputy chairman of the state committee on Securities and Exchanges of the Russian Federation, said that setting up a sound depository system and protecting investors right are the goals of a new commission.
He conceded that the current Russian legal framework needs improvement which may take some time.
But with the draft securities law pending for discussion in the Duma, progess is being made, he said.

Koleshnikov emphasized that with the re-election of President Boris Yeltsin for a second term, Russia has turned a corner for political and economic stability, which reduces risk for investing in Russians.
The development of the Russian stock market will in turn bring more political and social stability to Russia, he said.
